findings.statement: Growers phone all day about their fruit, packout, payments and downgrades, and the co-op can't answer quickly because the information is spread over five or six places, some of it on paper, and growers can't see any of it.
In the season Marietjie takes 40 to 50 calls a day and Precious about 10 a day about grading, the angry ones; growers phone because they don't know where they stand for weeks.

At the weighbridge, WeighMate prints the truck's weight on a slip and the clerk copies it onto a handwritten three-copy carbon delivery ticket with the grower number, farm, orchard block, cultivar and number of bins; bins get a cardboard tag with the ticket number.
Growers' bins get mixed up when cardboard tags fall off or ticket numbers are misread, two or three times a week in the peak, and each case takes a day to sort out.

The Optisort optical grader sorts fruit into class one (export), class two (local) and juice and produces a packout report per batch (one delivery ticket); Marietjie prints the reports daily and types the totals into the spreadsheet.

Sipho's spreadsheet has a row per delivery and is used to calculate monthly advance payments per carton of class one and two and per bin of juice, with a final pool payment once a year in February; payments go out via a bank batch file and the totals are journalled into LedgerOne monthly.

Growers' statements are made in the spreadsheet, printed and posted or emailed, and reach them about three weeks or more after the month ends, because everything is typed, checked and reconciled first.
Maturity test results from the QC lab are on paper and sent to growers as a WhatsApp photo; spray records arrive by paper, email or WhatsApp and are filed in a lever arch file.
Halve the growers' phone calls, and send statements within five working days after the month ends instead of about three weeks.
Growers can see their own deliveries and packout on their phones the same day or the day after.
Bins are traceable by scanning them at intake and again at the tipper, where they are tipped into the water, instead of by cardboard tags that fall off in the rain.

Marietjie, who types for three to four hours a day in the season and knows the spreadsheet and the growers, retires at the end of June 2027, in the middle of the first season with the new system, with no replacement yet; she should take part in testing before she goes.
Intake at the weighbridge must keep working without the network and catch up when the link is back; trucks can never be stopped at the gate.

The weighbridge, 300 metres from the office, is on a wireless link that drops about once a week for an hour in the season (heavy rain, or the gate battery running flat in load-shedding), and the area's fibre sometimes fails, once for a full day last year. Ruan will fit a bigger battery at the gate, but can't fix the fibre outages.
WeighMate is old: it runs on a Windows PC under the counter at the gate, writes every weighing to a database file and can export a CSV at the end of the day.

The Optisort grader's computer is locked down, its reports are PDFs and touching it would void the support contract, so getting packout data out automatically is uncertain and could slip; if it does, Marietjie keeps typing for a while.

Can the Optisort grader's agent provide an export (CSV or API), and at what cost? Ruan will email them this week. If not, someone types the totals from the reports as now, or the PDF reports might be read automatically if they hold real text in a fixed layout; Precious will send sample grader reports.
The advance payment calculation stays in Sipho's spreadsheet for phase one, because the board changes the rates every season; the new system supplies the deliveries and packout as an export.
A monthly export for Sipho's spreadsheet with totals per grower, per cultivar and per class, with the delivery numbers alongside, not one row per bin.
A daily summary for management of the previous day's bins received and packout per cultivar, emailed at 06:00 and on a page Johan can look at, also when he is away.
Do statements come from the new system (with Sipho uploading the advances each month) or stay in the spreadsheet?
Each grower sees only their own deliveries, packouts and statements; growers must never see each other's payments.

Roles: the office and management see everything; packhouse staff see deliveries and grading but not bank details or payments; growers see their own. Grower records include ID numbers, bank details, addresses and contact details (personal information under POPIA).
Bank details, and growers' phone numbers, are changed only by the office (bank details by Sipho with a letter from the bank), never by the grower from their phone, after an attempted fraud last year.
Every change to a delivery (weight, bin count) is recorded: who, when, the value before and the reason; the grower sees that a delivery was corrected.
findings.note: Whether the grower also sees the reason is left open (T142 to T145).

findings.statement: Should the grower see the reason a delivery was corrected, or only that it was?
The system is hosted in the cloud in a South African data centre (the board requires the data to stay in South Africa), not on a server in the office.
The weighbridge tablet needs a PIN or login and holds only what it needs (the day's deliveries and the grower list, not bank details), in case it is stolen.
Deliveries and statements are kept for five years (the auditors' rule), including for growers who leave.
findings.note: Flagging leavers' records for deletion after five years is only the consultant's suggestion (B72).

findings.statement: Growers' pages must work on cheap Android phones over slow connections without using much data, as a web page opened from a link (savable to the home screen), not an app to download.
When a batch is graded, the grower gets an SMS with the packout (for example 78% class one) and a link; SMS first, WhatsApp perhaps later. Ruan thinks an SMS costs about 25 to 30 cents.
Growers log in with a code sent by SMS to the phone number on file, with no passwords.
Should the grower pages also be in Xitsonga (and perhaps Afrikaans)? English is the minimum, and statements must be in English for the auditors; the consultant will price the translation.
The co-op's colours (orange and dark green) and logo, big clear writing for older members, and simple grower pages: deliveries, packout and statements, not much else.
At the weighbridge, a rugged tablet rather than the PC, with big buttons usable with gloves and a screen readable in the sun; at the tipper, as close to one button as possible.
Intake prints a small slip for each grower on the truck for the driver to take away; the carbon books stay as a fallback if the tablet fails, with a quick way to enter those tickets afterwards.
At the peak, 60 to 70 trucks a day, mostly between 07:00 and 11:00, carrying 6 to 40 bins each; 2,400 bins on the peak day last season and about 1,800 on a normal mid-season day.
findings.note: T221's 1,800 at the peak is corrected at T228.

findings.statement: Capturing a delivery should take the clerk under a minute (it takes four to five minutes now, and the queue backs up onto the road).

Up to 162 member growers would use the portal (140 delivered last season; the others can come back any time), and the big farms have several users each (owner, manager, perhaps a bookkeeper), so a few hundred users at most.
findings.note: Johan's 'a hundred and forty' (T11, T234) is corrected by Sipho at T235.

findings.statement: A grower's page loads in about three seconds on a 3G connection.

One truck can carry several growers' bins (a contractor collects from six or seven small growers); intake splits the truck's net weight across growers by number of bins, and each grower's ticket shows his share. The contractor, paid by the growers directly, needs nothing from the system.

Scanning a bin at the tipper shows the grower, block and cultivar, and tells the operator when a delivery's last bin has gone in so the grader batch is closed; today the foreman shouts it and batches get mixed.
Buying an off-the-shelf packhouse system was ruled out three years ago: about R2 million plus a yearly licence, far more than a co-op this size needs, and none of the small-grower features.

The grower list with its orchard blocks and cultivars (about 600 blocks, partly out of date, checked by Marietjie) is brought over from the spreadsheet; last season's deliveries only if cheap, to be decided once the consultant has seen the spreadsheet.

The board approved up to R580,000 excluding VAT for development and up to R4,500 a month in running costs (resolution of 21 August). The financial year ends in February, so most should be paid, in stages, before then.
findings.note: Johan's R650,000 at T275 is corrected from the resolution at T282.

findings.statement: The R4,500 a month covers everything it takes to run the system, including SMSes and hosting; the resolution doesn't say.
Hardware: three rugged tablets at about R8,500 each and a slip printer at about R2,000, shown as a separate line and probably paid from the equipment budget; Sipho to check with the auditor.
Weighbridge intake live by 1 March 2027 (first mandarins at the end of March); grower pages by the end of April 2027.
Growers upload their spray records for each orchard block on the portal; export buyers test for residues and the auditors check the records.
If a grower's spray records are missing, the delivery is still accepted but marked not for export, with a warning at the weighbridge and at the tipper scan.
Do the auditors accept digital spray records? Johan will ask them; their next audit is in May.
Does the grower see the packout straight from the grader, or only after Precious has checked the report (which would make her a bottleneck at about 60 batches a day in the peak)?
A grower can raise a query on a delivery from their page, which reaches Precious with the delivery, scans and grader report; phoning stays possible, and she sees how many queries each grower sends.

The 2005 membership forms say nothing about POPIA; update them or send members a notice about the portal and SMSes before the season, with the wording checked by the lawyer member. Johan is the registered information officer.
Who at the co-op looks after the system day to day (adding growers and clerks, resetting tablets)? Perhaps Marietjie's replacement; Johan will come back on it before training.

In the season the grower pages must be up on working days including Saturdays (the packhouse works Saturday mornings in the peak, when growers have time to look); an hour down is acceptable, a day is not. The consultant proposed 06:00 to 18:00, Monday to Saturday, with maintenance at night or out of season.
If the small growers don't use the portal, the calls won't go down; mitigated by showing it at study group days and with the extension officer, Mister Baloyi, who visits every second week.
The portal is launched to growers at the AGM on 11 March, then each grower gets an SMS with a link from the office, with Mister Baloyi and Marietjie helping those who get stuck.

Training in February with practice days on made-up deliveries: two sessions for the packhouse team (shifts) and one for the office; a short manual with pictures; the consultant on site for the first two mornings of the season.
A fixed price for phase one, with the grader connection priced separately.
Support through the first season, including Saturday mornings, priced in the proposal.
See the main grower screens designed first and reviewed with some growers before anything is built, and a half-hour progress update every two weeks showing working software, not slides.
The intake screen also records the truck registration and the driver's name, replacing the guard's book (a small extra).
Maturity test results from the QC lab in the system, later, not in phase one.
A possible merger with the Blyde co-op in Hoedspruit (about 60 growers) would add a second packhouse in two or three years; the data should allow more than one packhouse.
Later: export documents per container (now in spreadsheets), and the annual pool payment calculation if phase one works.
Tracking the co-op's own bins, about 100 of which are lost each year.

How will bins be labelled for scanning? Most bins belong to the growers, some numbered and some not; the co-op lends out about 3,000 of its own bins with numbers burnt in; Precious floated a clip-on plastic barcode tag that comes back to the weighbridge, and the consultant will look into what other packhouses do.
Ruan thinks the weighbridge's scale indicator is connected to the PC by a serial cable, so the weight could probably be read live from the indicator, without WeighMate.
The board's monthly report (volumes, packout, advances paid), which takes Sipho a day by hand, stays in his spreadsheet in phase one, with the volumes and packout coming from the system.

The hosting and other accounts are in the co-op's name, not the developer's or Ruan's, with the consultant given access while working for the co-op; the last developer kept everything in his own name, and the co-op lost its website for two years.
The consultant suggested that the system keeps a leaver's records for five years and then flags them for deletion, with the co-op deciding; so far nobody has ever thrown anything away.

Packhouse users: two weighbridge clerks (one per shift, both together in the peak) and three tipper staff over the shifts, plus Precious and the foreman; the clerks are comfortable with WhatsApp and the WeighMate screen, the tipper staff less so.

Volume is growing: two new members are planting, and navel orchards are being replaced with mandarins (smaller fruit, more cartons per bin); the board's plan is 10% more volume a year for the next five years, though Johan isn't sure it will happen.

Bosveld Citrus packs oranges (Valencias and navels), lemons and mandarins for its member growers, from large commercial farms to small growers with five or six hectares, through one packhouse in Letsitele; the season runs from the end of March (early mandarins) to about mid-September (last Valencias).
findings.note: Johan's 'about a hundred and forty' growers at T11 is corrected to 162 members at T235 (B39); this finding gives no count.

findings.statement: Daily backups, kept in a second location that is also in South Africa.

Next to his own packout, a grower sees the average packout of all growers for that cultivar that week, never with another grower's name, and only when at least five growers delivered that cultivar that week; today growers phone Precious to compare.
The packout shows the size groups (large, medium, small) as well as the classes, for the grower and in Sipho's export, because prices and the board's advance rates differ per size group.
The grader's PDF reports include the fruit sizes on the second page; Precious will send samples with it. Getting the sizes depends on what the grader export gives or what the PDFs hold.

Big trucks are weighed in and out; bakkies and tractors with trailers use an empty (tare) weight from a list on the weighbridge office wall, which should be updated monthly but in practice is weighed only at the start of each season.
findings.note: T396 corrects 'every month' to what actually happens: once a season.

findings.statement: The system keeps each vehicle's empty weight and warns (not blocks) when it is more than a month old, so the clerk weighs that vehicle out and records the new tare; otherwise a grower can be paid for a heavier trailer.

Mandarins wait two to three days in the four degreening rooms and oranges wait in rows in the holding area, where a delivery sometimes gets forgotten behind the others: last season twelve bins of Nadorcotts sat in the holding area for six days, went soft and went to juice, through the co-op's fault.
A list of deliveries waiting in the holding area and degreening rooms, oldest first, showing the room, with anything waiting more than three days shown in red.
Who records that a delivery has moved into a degreening room, and where is it scanned? Not the forklift driver; perhaps someone at the room doors. The consultant will come back with options.
The Wi-Fi doesn't reach inside the degreening rooms (insulated panel walls); scanning at their doors would need another outdoor access point, about R5,000 to R6,000 with cabling.

The consultant proposed that the tipper screen holds its scans when the network drops and sends them when it is back, as at the weighbridge: in load-shedding the packhouse generator takes about 30 seconds to start, the Wi-Fi drops meanwhile, and the access points sometimes take two more minutes to come back.
Ruan will put a small UPS (about R3,000) on the packhouse Wi-Fi access points; Johan approved it.

A weekly report for the export agent in Durban of cartons packed per cultivar and class, ready by 09:00 on Monday in the agent's template; the agent plans the ships from it, so late numbers mean the fruit misses a ship. Sipho now spends an hour to an hour and a half on it every Monday.
findings.note: Sipho's 'every Friday' is corrected to Monday morning at T430.

findings.statement: The cold store (pallets with their own numbers, tracked in the cold store manager's book) stays out of phase one; the agent will probably want it later.
Only about 130 to 135 growers have a good cellphone number on file; about 30 have none, a landline, or the number of someone who has died, and need checking before the season.

When several growers share one phone (for example the Mathebula family, three grower numbers on one phone), does whoever has the phone see all of them, or does each grower need his own number? Sipho will ask the lawyer member.

Statements show the advance less deductions: a packing fee per carton, bin hire for co-op bins (R35 per bin per season), transport for the few who use the co-op's truck, and levies, with last month next to this month; Sipho will send a sample with a fake name.

Big farms could optionally give notice on their page of the bins coming the next day (they now WhatsApp Precious), to help plan the line; a nice-to-have for a later phase unless cheap, and never compulsory.

For the first two weeks of the season the weighbridge runs the carbon books and the tablet side by side, with an extra temporary clerk, and Sipho checks the first month's export against the spreadsheet before paying growers.

Growers can propose changes to their orchard blocks (cultivar, planting year, hectares) on their page, and the office approves them, because the spray records follow the block; today the co-op finds out only when the wrong cultivar arrives.

Collecting growers' February crop estimates (bins expected per cultivar, which the board wants before the season; now on paper forms that Marietjie chases) on their page: in phase one if there is time, otherwise next season, priced separately.

notFindings.why: The consent check at the start of the meeting is recorded on the consent form, not in the record.
Small talk about the road works on the R71.
Ruan arriving late and the mix-up about the time; introductions, not findings.
A tangent about last Saturday's hailstorm; nothing for the system.

The consultant's own follow-ups (summary by Friday, proposal in two weeks) and the summary of who does what are actions, not findings about the client; the open items they refer to are already in the key.
Ruan's idea of counting fruit with drones, dismissed by Johan ('Not today'); only the advance notice of deliveries that follows it (B93) is a finding.
